messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Editor
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin, Female Presence: Being alone with women, Dissociative Feeling: Beginning to feel detached or unreal
  Memory: Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
  Negative Appraisals: Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Sameer Patel was twenty-four when the warrant called him into the refrigerated storage room of a struggling warehouse on the edge of Indianapolis. The air had bit through his uniform the moment the heavy steel door groaned open, hitting his forearms with a biting, metallic chill that never truly left his skin. Inside, a woman stood between him and a weeping child, her movements erratic and desperate. The cold air carried the sharp, chemical scent of industrial antifreeze that clung to his nostrils. When she lunged, Sameer’s training had taken over, but the sudden crack of the rifle and the woman’s collapse fractured his world. He was forced to drop to the pavement of the loading dock, his weight settling exactly onto his right knee and left thigh, a posture his body would never forget. In the months that followed, the warehouse night replayed behind his eyelids. Whenever the memory surfaced, an overwhelming grief would flood his chest, so heavy he could barely draw breath. He would suddenly smell that same acrid antifreeze, though he was miles away from any cold storage facility. His hands would tremble as his muscles locked into that exact loading dock posture, knees bent, shoulders hunched, as if the ground were still shaking beneath him. Each time the grief and the phantom scent rose, the chilling sensation on his skin intensified, pulling him back into the room where it had all gone wrong. The sensory echoes were relentless, turning ordinary moments into ambushes that left him trembling in place. Now working as an editor at a downtown publishing house, Sameer found himself trapped in those same ambushes. The building’s climate control was notoriously erratic, and on the day the thermostat suddenly dropped, plunging the editing suite into a familiar, biting cold, his skin prickled with that exact temperature. He was left alone with a freelance copyeditor reviewing a manuscript, and her quiet presence in the closed room triggered a wave of acute dread. As the chill crept up his arms and the memory of the loading dock seized him, Sameer began to interpret his own collapse as proof that he was fundamentally broken. He had come to believe his nervous system was a lousy coper that failed him when he needed it most. When the memories of the shooting finally broke through the dissociation, they brought the crushing grief again, which only reinforced his conviction that nothing good could happen to him anymore. The trauma felt like a permanent verdict on his competence, draining the purpose from his days until nothing in his work felt meaningful. The self-doubt quickly fed back into his sensory world. Once he started viewing himself as a failure, his mind turned inward, actively mining his past for confirmation, and that self-criticism pulled the vivid memories of the loading dock back into his awareness. That relentless self-criticism made the temperature on his skin feel like a countdown, heightening his panic until he was already feeling detached and unreal before he even left the office. The dissociation would deepen into a hazy distance, making the world feel paper-thin and untouchable. A single clause here or there—like noticing a dropped pen or a flickering fluorescent bulb—would briefly remind him of the event, but it never anchored his attention. The cycle tightened with every passing week; the more he feared his own reactions, the more his body prepared for the cold, and the more the memories arrived unbidden, each reinforcing his certainty that he was doomed to repeat the same paralysis. By the time Sameer walked into the clinic, the habit of avoidance had hollowed out his marriage. He stopped answering texts from his wife when the office thermostat clicked down, and he avoided meeting her female friends for coffee after the detached feeling took hold. What finally drove him to seek help was a panic attack in his own kitchen, where the sudden drop in evening temperature locked his body into the loading dock posture and left him unable to speak to his wife. He sat on the edge of the examination table now, his hands resting heavily on his knees, terrified that the grief would never leave and that his life had permanently lost its forward motion. He was hoping, despite his certainty that nothing good could happen to him, that he might finally find a way to steady his breathing and return to the stories he used to love editing.
